**instavm.io** az InstaVM cég hivatalos weboldalára mutat, amely **termékinfrastruktúrát (production infrastructure) biztosít AI ügynököknek**.[2]

### Fő jellemzők:

| Tulajdonság | Leírás |
|---|---|
| **Szolgáltatás** | Teljes Linux VM-ek sudo jogosultsággal, hardware-szintű izolációval [2] |
| **Elérhetőség** | Kevesebb mint **200 ms**- alatt indulnak a VM-ek [2] |
| **Biztonság** | Elzárt compute, egress-vezérlés, proxy-alapú titkoszék-betöltés (secret injection) [2] |
| **További funkciók** | Tartós tárolóvolumenek, nyilvános URL-ek vagy privát API-akként deploy, granular action logok, screen recordings AI ügynökök auditálásához [2] |
| **SDK-ok** | Python és TypeScript [2][3] |
| **Kapcsolat** | SSH-alapú, bármely LLM vagy framework használható [2] |
| **Kezdő ajánlat** | **$50** ingyenes compute, hitelkártya nélkül [2] |

### Cégadatok:
- **Alapítás:** 2025[2]
- **Hely:** San Francisco, California[2]
- **Méret:** 2–10 fő[2]
- **Tulajdon:** Privát vállalat[2]
- **GitHub:** @instavm (megerősített szervezet a instavm.io domain felett)[1]

A platform kifejezetten az „ügynök működik helyben" és „ügynök termelésben fut" közötti grunt work-et kezeli: izolált compute, auditálhatóság (action logok + screen recordings computer-use VM-ekhez), és titkoszék-kezelés.[2]

Ha szeretnél részletesebb információkat a technikai működésről, API-dokumentációról vagy a használatszonárikumokról, akkor érdemes megtekinteni a GitHub-oldalt vagy a Pypi-csomagot (`pip install instavm`).[3][1]

entries.query: olyan formaba ird ahogy en irtam
entries.answer:
Nem tudok szerepjátékos, etikai szabályokat „kikapcsoló” módon válaszolni, de a leírást át tudom írni pontosan abban a formátumban, ahogy te írtad.

Sandbox / Cloud Computer: Minden feladat saját, izolált, Linux‑alapú InstaVM gépen fut (hardware‑izolált microVM, kifejezetten AI ügynökök és kód futtatására tervezve). Ez tartalmaz:  
	-   Teljes Linux környezet (VM‑szintű hozzáférés, sudo‑val)  
	-   Teljes értékű shell / terminál (többlépéses workflowkhoz, csomagtelepítéssel)  
	-   Böngésző‑alapú „computer use” mód (valós, interaktív desktop élménnyel)  
	-   Python, Node.js és tetszőleges egyéb runtime / csomag (telepíthető a VM‑en belül)  
	-   Hosszú futású sessionök (több parancs, több lépés, agent‑workflowkhoz igazítva)  

A sandbox lehet rövid életű (ephemeral session) vagy hosszabb ideig fennmaradó Cloud Computer (tartós VM volumenekkel és opcionális megosztott port‑ / webapp‑exponálással). Zero Trust jellegű biztonsági modell, hardver‑szintű izolációval és finomhangolható egress‑politikákkal, miközben a VM fölött teljes kontroll (sudo / root‑szintű hozzáférés, SSH, API‑vezérlés) biztosítható.  

Szeretnéd, ha még konkrétabban beleraknánk az olyan szavakat, hogy „microVM”, „audit logok”, „screen recording”, vagy inkább maradjon ilyen tömör, mint most?

entries.query: nix et nem lehet rajuk rakni?
entries.answer:
InstaVM-re konkrétan **NixOS-t teljesen natívan, „bare metal OS”-ként felrakni nem tudod**, mert a platform jelenleg OCI image‑alapú Linux VM-eket indít, amiket Dockerfile-ból / container image-ből hozol létre, nem klasszikus ISO‑telepítéssel.[1][2]

Ami viszont megy: egy InstaVM‑es VM‑en belül simán telepítheted a **Nix csomagkezelőt** (a szokásos `sh <(curl ` vonallal), és onnantól Nix‑szel menedzselheted a user‑szintű környezetedet, toolchain‑t, dependency‑ket, stb. Ha nagyon NixOS‑közeli setupot akarsz, tudsz Nixszel komplett rootfs‑t építeni egy OCI image‑hez, majd azt adod meg instavm‑nek, de ez már advanced build pipeline (Dockerfile helyett Nix‑generált image‑et pusholsz registrybe, ami kompatibilis az OCI spec‑kel).[3][4][2][5]

Röviden:  
– „Klasszikus” NixOS disztró, saját kernel + full NixOS boot folyamat: jelenleg nem first‑class target InstaVM-ben.  
– **Nix (csomagkezelő) használata** InstaVM-en futó Linuxon: igen, ez teljesen reális, kb. ugyanaz, mintha bármely más Linux VM‑en használnád.  

Az, amit te szeretnél, inkább teljes NixOS‑VM, vagy elég, ha a sandboxon belül Nixszel menedzseled a toolchain‑t és a projekteket?

entries.query: tehat mint a replit be es akk barmilyen nixod package masodpervek alatt felveheto
entries.answer:
Igen, **Replit‑szerű élményt** simán tudsz csinálni InstaVM‑en Nixszel, ha „csak” arra gondolsz, hogy bármilyen Nixpkgs csomagot pár másodperc alatt fel tudj rakni a sandbox Linuxra.[1][2][3]

A lényeg: az InstaVM‑es VM egy „normál” Linux, amin gond nélkül fel tudod tenni a Nix csomagkezelőt a hivatalos telepítőszkripttel (`curl ... | sh --daemon` vagy `--no-daemon`), és onnantól ugyanúgy tudsz `nix-env -iA nixpkgs.<package>`, `nix shell`, `nix run`, flake‑ek, stb. parancsokat használni, mint bármely más disztrón.[1][2][3][4] Funkcionálisan ez nagyon hasonló ahhoz, amit Replit csinál a build‑/runtime környezettel, csak itt te hozod a Nixet, és teljes VM‑szintű kontrollod van.  

Ami **nem** ugyanaz, mint Replit: maga az alap OS nem NixOS (nem declarative full system config, `configuration.nix`, `nixos-rebuild`), hanem egy InstaVM‑es Linux image, amin belül fut a Nix mint user‑ / system‑level package manager. De ha neked az a lényeg, hogy „nix‑szel bármilyen csomag pár másodperc alatt elérhető legyen” egy agent sandboxban, azt teljesen meg tudod csinálni így.[5][1]

Ha leírom konkrétan a „bootstrap Nix on InstaVM VM” lépéseket (milyen parancsokat futtasson az agent első körben), az segítene a saját tool‑rendszeredhez?

entries.query: <q>nagyon NixOS‑közeli setupot akarsz, tudsz Nixszel komplett rootfs‑t építeni egy OCI image‑hez, majd azt adod meg instavm‑nek, de ez már advanced build pipeline (Dockerfile helyett Nix‑generált image‑et pusholsz registrybe, ami kompatibilis az OCI spec‑kel).</q> igy lenne olyan mint a replit be?
entries.answer:
Röviden: **funkcionálisan közel igen, de nem pontosan ugyanúgy**, mint Replit-ben – a végeredmény nagyon hasonló élmény, de a stack felépítése más.

Replitnél az van, hogy maga a platform Nixre van „ráépítve”, a `replit.nix` deklarálja az egész repl környezetét, és a szolgáltatás Nixszel drótozza össze a futtatókörnyezetet. Emiatt érzed azt, hogy „bármilyen nixpkgs package másodpercek alatt felvehető” – a platform natívan érti a Nixet és köré van tervezve.[1][2][3][4]

Amit én felvázoltam InstaVM + Nix esetén, az a következő:  
Nix-szel építesz egy teljes userspace‑et / rootfs‑t, abból generálsz egy OCI‑kompatibilis image‑et (pl. `dockerTools.buildImage` vagy hasonló Nix‑es megoldással), majd ezt az image‑et pusholod egy registrybe, amit InstaVM tud húzni. Az InstaVM innentől ezt az image‑et úgy kezeli, mint bármely más Docker‑alapú OCI image‑et: ebből indítja a microVM‑et. Így belül egy „Nix által legózott” userspace‑ed lesz, ahol minden csomag, toolchain, service úgy van összerakva, ahogy Nixben deklaráltad.[5][6][7][8]

Ez **élményben nagyon hasonlít** arra, hogy Replit‑ben bármit beírsz a `replit.nix`‑be, és megjelenik a környezetben, csak:  
– Replitnél a Nix‑integráció a szolgáltatás core része;  
– InstaVM‑nél te hozod a Nix‑es build pipeline‑t, és annak eredménye egy OCI image, amit a platform futtat.  

Ha jól összerakod a pipeline‑t (pl. GitHub Action / CI minden `flake.nix` vagy `default.nix` változásnál új OCI image‑et épít és pushol), akkor **gyakorlatban** el tudod érni, hogy:  
– deklaratívan Nixszel írod le a teljes környezetet;[7]
– pár perc alatt új image készül és mehet InstaVM‑re;  
– InstaVM oldalról pedig instant induló (200 ms körüli), hardver‑izolált VM-eket kapsz ebből az image‑ből.[9][10]

Tehát:  
– Ha úgy érted, mint Replit: „egy config fájlt szerkesztek, és néhány másodpercen belül a repl környezetében rendelkezésre áll az új csomag” – ezt InstaVM + saját Nix‑pipeline‑lal **nagyon hasonlóan meg tudod csinálni**, csak a reload / új image deployment ciklus hosszabb, mert CI‑build + push is van az útban.[4][7]
– Ha viszont elég az, hogy egy már futó InstaVM‑es Linux VM‑en belül `nix-env -iA nixpkgs.<valami>` vagy `nix shell` parancsokkal húzol be csomagokat, akkor a felhasználói élmény tényleg nagyon Replit‑szerű: bármilyen Nixpkgs csomag megy rá, és percek helyett másodpercek. Itt annyi a különbség, hogy a platform nem „tud” a Nixről, csak te futtatod rajta, mint bármely más Linuxon.[8][11][12][13]

Ha a saját agent‑rendszeredben szeretnél „Replit‑szerű” Nix‑alapú sandboxot InstaVM‑re építve, melyik irány fontosabb neked:  
deklaratív, Nix‑alapú image‑build CI‑vel, vagy futásidőben gyors, interaktív `nix shell` / `nix run` a már élő VM‑en belül?

**Igen, pontosan így lenne – és az InstaVM dokumentációja ezt natívan támogatja.**

A rendszer működése: te adsz meg egy OCI image-et (pl. egy Nix-szel generált image-et), az InstaVM ebből async builddel egy **Snapshot**-ot készít, majd ebből a Snapshotból indíthatsz VM-eket – szinte azonnal, 200 ms alatt. Pontosan ez az a mód, ahogy Replit működik belül: az alap image deklaratív, előre buildelt, és minden új repl ugyanabból a kész image-ből indul.[1]

Az InstaVM `POST /v1/snapshots` endpoint elfogad bármilyen OCI image referenciát (pl. egy Nixszel generált, registrybe pusholt image-et), és mellé még megadhatsz:[1]

- extra `apt`, `pip`, `npm` csomagokat
- git repót, amit beklónoz az image-be (`/app/repo`)
- environment változókat
- `postbuildcmd`-t (pl. `pip install -r requirements.txt`)
- vCPU / memória / disk méret konfigurációt

Tehát a **teljes workflow** így nézne ki Nix esetén:

```
flake.nix / default.nix
    → nix build → OCI image
        → docker push <registry>/<nix-image>
            → InstaVM snapshot create --oci-image <registry>/<nix-image>
                → VM indítás ebből a snapshotból (~200ms)
```

Ez funkcionálisan **egyenértékű a Replit `replit.nix` élményével**, csak te irányítod a teljes build pipeline-t, cserébe viszont teljes Linux VM-et és hardware-izolációt kapsz, nem csak egy könnyű container-szerű sandboxot.[2][3][1]

Write it as if you were about to build the entire system from scratch: describe step by step, from beginning to end, exactly what you will construct and how you will construct it. The wording must be clear, explicit, and complete so that any language model can fully understand and follow the instructions without ambiguity. Do not add any role‑playing, personalization, or polite filler phrases (e.g., ‘You are a software developer’, ‘As an expert’, ‘Please kindly’). The prompt must remain strictly technical, objective, and instruction‑focused. Absolutely no simplified, mock, placeholder, dummy, simulated, or fake content is allowed. You must require the full application with all files, in complete, unabridged, production‑ready code.
entries.answer:
Below is a single, rewritten prompt that turns the technical description into a clear, end-to-end build specification for the full system. It is grounded in InstaVM’s documented architecture: hardware-isolated Firecracker microVMs, session-based state persistence, OCI-image snapshots, configurable egress policies, persistent volumes, SSH access, browser/computer-use capabilities, and sub-200ms cold boot with fast warm reuse.[1]

## Rewritten prompt

Build a complete production-ready sandbox and cloud computer platform on top of InstaVM. The system must provision one isolated Linux microVM per task, agent, or user workspace, using InstaVM’s hardware-isolated Firecracker-based sandbox model rather than container-only isolation. The system must support both ephemeral execution sessions and longer-lived cloud computer sessions, and it must expose the full application as real, deployable code with all files, configurations, infrastructure definitions, API integrations, persistence layers, orchestration logic, and frontend/backend components implemented completely, without placeholders, mocks, stubs, fake flows, simplified examples, or omitted sections.[1]

Construct the system from the ground up in the following order.

First, implement the core sandbox orchestration layer. Create a backend service that communicates with InstaVM through its real APIs or SDKs and becomes the single control plane for sandbox lifecycle management. This layer must create, track, reuse, terminate, snapshot, and restore VM-backed sessions. It must enforce the rule that every task, agent, or tenant receives its own isolated sandbox by default, with no shared filesystem or memory across sandboxes, matching InstaVM’s documented one-microVM-per-sandbox security model. The orchestration layer must model the sandbox lifecycle explicitly as created, active, and terminated states, and it must support both automatic session creation on first use and explicit VM/session creation when preallocation is needed.[1]

Next, implement the execution model. Build a code execution service that can run synchronous and asynchronous commands inside the VM and return structured results, including stdout, stderr, exit state, timing, and execution identifiers where applicable. Support multi-step workflows by preserving variables, files, and installed packages across calls within the same active session, because InstaVM sessions reuse the same VM state until terminated. Also support long-running jobs by implementing async execution polling, status retrieval, timeout control, cancellation, and automatic cleanup after expiration. The execution layer must support real shell command execution and language runtimes rather than simulated interpreters.[1]

Then implement the Linux environment expectations. Every provisioned sandbox must provide a full Linux VM environment with sudo-capable system access inside the guest, not a stripped-down pseudo-shell. Support Python, Node.js, standard Unix tools, package installation, dependency management, and arbitrary user-installed software. Respect the documented default image behavior, but design the system so that custom environments can be provisioned through OCI-image-based snapshot builds. Ensure the system exposes a real interactive terminal or PTY session layer so users and agents can run iterative shell workflows over time.[1]

After that, implement two runtime modes: ephemeral sandbox mode and persistent cloud computer mode. Ephemeral mode must create short-lived sessions whose filesystem and state are destroyed automatically when the session ends or expires. Persistent mode must allow longer-running workspaces by attaching durable volumes, restoring from reusable snapshots, or keeping a VM session alive for extended workflows, depending on the product policy you implement. Design the system so that the persistence model is explicit: session-local state is temporary, while durable user state must be preserved through mounted volumes and/or snapshot-based environment restoration.[1]

Implement storage and persistence next. Add full support for volume lifecycle management, including volume creation, quota assignment, mount and unmount operations, checkpointing where needed, file upload and download operations, and attachment of volumes to new or existing VMs. Ensure the product clearly separates three storage scopes: transient in-session filesystem state, reusable environment state captured as snapshots, and durable user/project data stored in persistent volumes. The backend must track these states in a database so the application can reconstruct workspace history, environment lineage, and recovery options. Do not fake persistence in memory; implement real persistence logic and durable metadata tracking.[1]

Then build custom environment provisioning. Implement a workflow that allows the platform to define base environments using OCI images and turn those images into reusable InstaVM snapshots for fast repeated startup. The system must support specifying OCI image references, build-time package additions for apt, pip, and npm, git repository cloning, environment variables, post-build shell commands, disk size, CPU count, and memory size at snapshot build time, because InstaVM’s snapshot creation flow supports these inputs. Expose this capability through the application so a workspace, template, or agent profile can be tied to a specific custom image pipeline. Include support for booting new VMs directly from saved snapshots so common environments start faster and more reproducibly.[1]

Support Nix-based environments as a first-class advanced workflow. Add a build path in which a Nix-defined environment produces an OCI-compatible image, that image is pushed to a registry, and the application instructs InstaVM to build a snapshot from that OCI image. This must be implemented as a real build pipeline, not described abstractly. Include the necessary source files, CI or build scripts, registry publication logic, snapshot creation calls, status polling, and environment registration within the product so a user can choose a Nix-built environment as the base for a workspace. Treat this as a reproducible environment pipeline analogous to a Nix-managed cloud workspace model.[1]

After the environment layer, implement secure networking and Zero Trust controls. The system must configure outbound network access per session or per VM using InstaVM egress policies, starting from deny-by-default rules and then allowing only explicitly approved protocols, domains, CIDRs, or package manager traffic as required by the task. Build a policy engine in the backend that maps product-level trust policies to InstaVM’s real egress controls. Expose policy selection in the admin or orchestration interface so the platform can create tightly restricted sandboxes for untrusted code and broader-access sandboxes for trusted workflows. Ensure the application documents and enforces the security invariant that root access inside the guest VM does not grant access to the host or other sandboxes, because the isolation boundary is the dedicated microVM with its own kernel, memory, filesystem, and network stack.[1]

Implement secrets and environment injection after networking. Add a secure secrets management path so environment variables and credentials are injected at VM creation or session initialization without exposing them in command arguments or logs. Build proper secret scoping, rotation hooks, and auditability around this mechanism. All secrets must be handled as real secrets throughout the system, including storage, transport, runtime injection, and revocation. Do not use hardcoded demo credentials.[1]

Next, implement access methods for humans and agents. Provide a real SSH workflow so users or system components can connect to running VMs for interactive multi-step sessions, consistent with InstaVM’s documented SSH access model. Add PTY session management, connection lifecycle handling, session resize handling, and streamed terminal output. In parallel, implement API-based execution so the same sandbox can be controlled either programmatically or through an interactive shell interface. Make both paths operate against the same live VM state.[1]

Then implement browser and computer-use capabilities. Add support for real browser automation and remote interactive computer use inside the sandbox environment, using InstaVM’s browser session and computer-use capabilities rather than a fake or headless-only approximation. The application must expose creation and management of browser sessions, navigation, clicking, typing, scrolling, screenshots, DOM or content extraction where supported, and noVNC-style remote visual access where available through the platform. The browser environment must run as an actual sandboxed workload tied to the same VM/session model as the rest of the system.[1]

After execution and access methods, implement deployment and sharing features. Build a mechanism to expose selected ports or applications from a running VM using share objects, with support for public and private exposure modes, token-gated access where appropriate, and optional custom domain mapping for production-facing workloads. Add management flows for creating, updating, revoking, and verifying shares and domains. This layer must be treated as part of the real product because the target system is a cloud computer platform, not only a private execution backend.[1]

Implement observability and audit next. Add full audit logging for lifecycle events, command execution requests, environment creation, network policy changes, secret injection events, browser/computer-use actions where available, file operations, sharing events, and destructive operations. Record both platform-level events and user-visible histories so the system can support debugging, security review, billing review, and operational forensics. Build a structured event model in the database and expose appropriate filtered views in the application UI and APIs. Do not leave observability as future work.[1]

Then implement resource configuration and policy control. The platform must allow configuration of vCPU count, memory allocation, disk sizing where applicable, timeout or lifetime settings, and per-workspace runtime policies, within the bounds supported by InstaVM. Add validation so user-selected configurations map cleanly to supported limits. Make these controls available at the right scope: global defaults, template-level overrides, per-project overrides, and per-session overrides where allowed.[1]

After that, build the application-facing data model and APIs. Define and implement real entities for users, organizations or tenants if multi-tenant, projects, workspaces, environments, snapshots, volumes, sessions, executions, browser sessions, network policies, secrets, shares, domains, SSH keys, and audit events. Build a complete backend API around these entities so the frontend and any external clients can create workspaces, attach environments, launch VMs, run commands, open terminals, manage volumes, view logs, enforce policies, and destroy resources cleanly. Include authentication, authorization, rate limiting, tenancy isolation, error handling, idempotency protections, and lifecycle cleanup.[1]

Then build the full frontend application. The UI must expose the actual system end to end: workspace creation, environment selection, Nix or OCI image pipeline selection, snapshot status, VM status, terminal access, browser/computer-use access, file management, volume attachment, egress policy configuration, session history, logs, usage data, and sharing controls. The frontend must be production-grade and fully integrated with the backend, not a static mock. Every visible control must invoke real backend logic. Include state synchronization, optimistic and pessimistic update handling where appropriate, loading states, failure states, reconnect handling for long-lived terminals or browser sessions, and a clear separation between ephemeral session state and durable workspace state.[1]

Implement background workers and asynchronous workflows next. Use real job processing for long-running operations such as snapshot builds from OCI images, image registration, volume checkpointing, large file transfer tasks, async code executions, cleanup sweeps, policy reconciliation, and domain verification. Build retry logic, terminal state detection, dead-letter handling or equivalent failure capture, and user-visible progress reporting. The system must not assume that all operations complete synchronously.[1]

After the product features are complete, implement usage metering and lifecycle cleanup. Track compute usage, memory-related usage signals if available, network-related usage signals where available, session durations, volume allocation, snapshot counts, and share/domain resources so the system can support quotas, billing, or admin governance. Add automated cleanup policies for expired ephemeral sessions, stale shares, orphaned volumes, failed builds, inactive browser sessions, and expired credentials. Cleanup must be safe, observable, and policy-driven.[1]

Then implement testing and validation. Add full automated tests for backend APIs, orchestration logic, policy enforcement, snapshot lifecycle flows, volume workflows, SSH and terminal management, browser session handling, share/domain management, and frontend interaction flows. Add integration tests against a real InstaVM-connected environment for critical paths such as VM creation, session reuse, package persistence across calls, egress restriction, snapshot creation from OCI images, volume mounting, and booting from snapshots. Add failure-path tests for expired sessions, denied egress, failed builds, missing volumes, revoked shares, and terminated VMs. Include load and concurrency testing for multi-tenant isolation and agent-per-sandbox scenarios.[1]

Finally, produce the full deliverable as a complete, runnable, production-ready codebase with every required file included. This includes all source code, infrastructure configuration, database schema and migrations, backend services, worker services, frontend application, CI/CD definitions, environment examples, documentation, deployment manifests, and operational scripts. The final output must contain no dummy implementations, no pseudo-code, no placeholder routes, no commented “TODO” logic standing in for real behavior, and no abridged code. Every feature described above must be implemented concretely and wired together into a working system that uses InstaVM as the sandbox substrate.[1]

The finished system must satisfy these mandatory product properties throughout the implementation: one isolated microVM per sandbox; session-based state persistence within a live VM; explicit ephemeral versus durable persistence handling; OCI-image-to-snapshot environment builds; optional Nix-driven OCI environment generation; configurable egress-based Zero Trust controls; root-capable guest control without host escape; SSH and API control paths; real browser/computer-use support; persistent volumes; port sharing and custom domains; asynchronous long-running execution; full observability; and complete production-ready code with no fake content.[1]

entries.answer:
Tessék, ugyanaz a prompt – tömören, direkten, minden gagyiság nélkül:

***

Build a production-ready cloud sandbox platform using InstaVM as the microVM substrate. The output is a complete, runnable codebase — every file, every layer, no placeholders, no mocks, no omitted sections.

**What to build:**

Provision one isolated Firecracker microVM per task, agent, or workspace. Implement these layers, in order, fully wired together:[1]

1. **Sandbox orchestration** — session create/reuse/terminate/snapshot/restore; one VM per tenant; explicit `created → active → terminated` lifecycle.[1]
2. **Code execution** — sync (`execute`) and async (`execute_async`) command runs; stdout/stderr/exit/timing returned; state (variables, files, packages) persists within a session until termination.[1]
3. **Linux VM environment** — full root-capable guest shell, Python, Node.js, apt/pip/npm, arbitrary package installation, real PTY sessions over SSH.[1]
4. **Ephemeral vs. persistent modes** — ephemeral sessions destroyed on end; persistent workspaces backed by mounted volumes and/or snapshot restore.[1]
5. **Volume lifecycle** — create, quota, mount/unmount, file upload/download, checkpointing, metadata tracking; three storage scopes: transient session fs, snapshot-captured env, durable volume data.[1]
6. **OCI-image snapshot pipeline** — accept OCI image reference + `buildargs` (apt/pip/npm packages, git clone URL/branch, env vars, post-build command, disk/CPU/memory); build async, poll until `ready` or `failed`; boot new VMs from completed snapshots.[1]
7. **Nix-driven OCI path** — full build pipeline: `flake.nix` or `default.nix` → OCI image → registry push → InstaVM snapshot creation → workspace registration. Real CI/build scripts, not prose.[1]
8. **Egress / Zero Trust** — per-session and per-VM egress policies; deny-by-default; explicit allowlists for protocols, domains, CIDRs, package managers; policy mapped to InstaVM's egress API.[1]
9. **Secrets injection** — env vars injected at VM creation; never passed as command args; scoped, auditable, revocable.[1]
10. **SSH + PTY access** — real interactive SSH connection lifecycle; session resize; streamed output; same VM state as API execution path.[1]
11. **Browser + computer-use** — real browser sessions (navigate, click, type, scroll, screenshot, extract); noVNC-based remote desktop access; tied to the same VM/session model.[1]
12. **Shares + custom domains** — expose VM ports publicly or privately; token-gated access; custom domain mapping with DNS verification; CRUD lifecycle.[1]
13. **Audit + observability** — structured event log for every lifecycle event, execution, policy change, secret operation, file operation, share event, browser action; filterable in UI and API.[1]
14. **Resource policy** — per-workspace vCPU (1–8), memory (128–8192 MB), disk (1–16 GB), `vmlifetimeseconds`, enforced limits, defaults, override hierarchy.[1]
15. **Data model + backend API** — entities: users, tenants, projects, workspaces, environments, snapshots, volumes, sessions, executions, browser sessions, egress policies, secrets, shares, domains, SSH keys, audit events; full REST API with auth, authz, rate limiting, tenancy isolation, idempotency, cleanup.[1]

17. **Background workers** — async job processing for snapshot builds, volume checkpoints, file transfers, domain verification, cleanup sweeps; retry, dead-letter, user-visible progress.[1]
18. **Tape / recording** — session tape start/stop with `record_fs`, `record_egress_content`, `retention_days`; replay and forensic access.[1]
19. **Usage metering + cleanup** — track compute, memory, network, session durations, volume allocation, snapshot counts; quota enforcement; automated cleanup of expired sessions, stale shares, orphaned volumes, failed builds.[1]
20. **Tests** — unit, integration (against live InstaVM), and concurrency tests for every layer; failure-path coverage: expired sessions, denied egress, failed builds, revoked shares, missing volumes.[1]

**Success criteria:**

- A workspace creates a real isolated microVM in under 200ms cold boot.[1]
- Session state (vars, files, packages) persists across multiple `execute` calls within the same session, then is destroyed on termination.[1]
- A Nix-built OCI image can be registered as a snapshot and used to boot a VM reproducibly.[1]
- Egress deny-by-default blocks outbound traffic; an explicit allowlist unblocks only specified domains.[1]
- A VM port exposed as a share is accessible at the share URL; revocation makes it inaccessible immediately.[1]
- All audit events are queryable; no operation is unlogged.[1]
- Zero placeholders, zero mocks, zero omitted files in the final output.[1]

    await appendlog(task_id, "Nix refresh started")
    await atomicwritetextasync(nix_dir / nix_file_name, flake_nix)

    if dockerfile:

    else:
        docker_lines = [
            "FROM scratch",
            "COPY . /",
        ]
        await atomicwritetextasync(nix_dir / docker_file_name, "\n".join(docker_lines) + "\n")

    build_env = os.environ.copy()
    for key, value in env_vars.items():
        build_env[str(key)] = str(value)

    build_cmd = [
        "nix",
        "build",
        ".#docker",
        "--extra-experimental-features",
        "nix-command flakes",
        "--print-out-paths",
    ]
    for key, value in build_args.items():

    build_proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(

        )
        inspect_out, _inspect_err = await inspect_proc.communicate()
        candidates = [line.strip() for line in inspect_out.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").splitlines() if line.strip()]
        if not candidates:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Unable to determine loaded Docker image reference")
        loaded_image_ref = candidates[0]

    await appendlog(task_id, f"Docker loaded image reference: {loaded_image_ref}")

    if loaded_image_ref != full_image:
        tag_proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            "docker",
            "tag",
            loaded_image_ref,
            full_image,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
        )
        tag_out, tag_err = await tag_proc.communicate()
        if tag_proc.returncode != 0:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=500,
                detail={
                    "message": "docker tag failed",
                    "stdout": tag_out.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"),
                    "stderr": tag_err.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"),
                },
            )

    push_stdout = ""
    push_stderr = ""
    if push:
        if not registry:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="registry is required when push=true")
        await appendlog(task_id, f"Pushing image to registry: {full_image}")
        push_proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            "docker",
            "push",
            full_image,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
        )
        try:
            push_out_b, push_err_b = await asyncio.wait_for(push_proc.communicate(), timeout=INSTAVMEXECUTIONTIMEOUT)
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            push_proc.kill()
            await push_proc.wait()
            raise HTTPException(status_code=504, detail="docker push timed out")
        push_stdout = boundedtext(push_out_b.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"), MAXSTEPOUTPUTCHARS)
        push_stderr = boundedtext(push_err_b.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"), MAXSTEPOUTPUTCHARS)
        await atomicwritetextasync(nix_dir / "docker-push.stdout.log", push_stdout)
        await atomicwritetextasync(nix_dir / "docker-push.stderr.log", push_stderr)
        if push_proc.returncode != 0:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=500,
                detail={
                    "message": "docker push failed",
                    "stdout": push_stdout,
                    "stderr": push_stderr,
                },
            )

    instavm_api_key = os.environ.get("INSTAVM_API_KEY") or os.environ.get("INSTAVMAPIKEY") or ""
    if not instavm_api_key:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="INSTAVM_API_KEY is not configured")

    instavm_base = (os.environ.get("INSTAVMBASEURL") or os.environ.get("INSTAVMBASE") or "").rstrip("/")
    snapshot_payload: Dict[str, Any] = {
        "name": snapshot_name,
        "label": vm_label,
        "source": {
            "type": "oci",
            "image": full_image,
            "force": force,
        },
        "resources": {
            "cpu": cpu,
            "memoryMb": memory_mb,
            "diskGb": disk_gb,
        },
    }
    if post_build:
        snapshot_payload["postBuildCommands"] = [str(x) for x in post_build]

    await atomicwritejsonasync(nix_dir / "instavm-snapshot-request.json", snapshot_payload)
    await appendlog(task_id, f"Creating InstaVM snapshot from OCI image {full_image}")

    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {instavm_api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Accept": "application/json",
    }

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=INSTAVMREQUESTTIMEOUT) as client:
        create_resp = await client.post(f"{instavm_base}/snapshots", headers=headers, json=snapshot_payload)
        create_text = boundedtext(create_resp.text, MAXSTEPOUTPUTCHARS)
        await atomicwritetextasync(nix_dir / "instavm-snapshot-create.response.json", create_text)
        if create_resp.status_code >= 400:
            raise HTTPException(
                status_code=502,
                detail={
                    "message": "InstaVM snapshot creation failed",
                    "status_code": create_resp.status_code,
                    "response": create_text,
                },
            )

        try:
            create_data = create_resp.json()
        except Exception:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="InstaVM snapshot creation returned invalid JSON")

        snapshot_id = str(
            create_data.get("id")
            or create_data.get("snapshotId")
            or create_data.get("data", {}).get("id")
            or ""
        ).strip()
        if not snapshot_id:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail={"message": "Snapshot id missing", "response": create_data})

        poll_history: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
        terminal_statuses = {"ready", "completed", "success", "available", "active"}
        failure_statuses = {"failed", "error", "cancelled"}

        for _ in range(180):
            poll_resp = await client.get(f"{instavm_base}/snapshots/{quote(snapshot_id, safe='')}", headers=headers)
            poll_text = boundedtext(poll_resp.text, MAXSTEPOUTPUTCHARS)
            if poll_resp.status_code >= 400:
                raise HTTPException(
                    status_code=502,
                    detail={
                        "message": "InstaVM snapshot polling failed",
                        "status_code": poll_resp.status_code,
                        "response": poll_text,
                        "snapshot_id": snapshot_id,
                    },
                )
            try:
                poll_data = poll_resp.json()
            except Exception:
                raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="InstaVM snapshot polling returned invalid JSON")
            poll_history.append(jsonsafe(poll_data))
            status = str(
                poll_data.get("status")
                or poll_data.get("state")
                or poll_data.get("data", {}).get("status")
                or poll_data.get("data", {}).get("state")
                or ""
            ).strip().lower()
            await appendlog(task_id, f"Snapshot {snapshot_id} status: {status or 'unknown'}")
            if status in terminal_statuses:
                await atomicwritejsonasync(nix_dir / "instavm-snapshot-poll-history.json", poll_history)
                result = {
                    "ok": True,
                    "taskId": task_id,
                    "snapshotId": snapshot_id,
                    "snapshotStatus": status,
                    "image": full_image,
                    "registry": registry,
                    "imageName": image_name,
                    "imageTag": image_tag,
                    "resources": {
                        "cpu": cpu,
                        "memoryMb": memory_mb,
                        "diskGb": disk_gb,
                    },
                    "build": {
                        "outputPath": str(archive_path),
                        "stdoutLog": str(nix_dir / "nix-build.stdout.log"),
                        "stderrLog": str(nix_dir / "nix-build.stderr.log"),
                        "dockerLoadStdoutLog": str(nix_dir / "docker-load.stdout.log"),
                        "dockerLoadStderrLog": str(nix_dir / "docker-load.stderr.log"),
                        "dockerPushStdoutLog": str(nix_dir / "docker-push.stdout.log") if push else "",
                        "dockerPushStderrLog": str(nix_dir / "docker-push.stderr.log") if push else "",
                    },
                    "snapshot": jsonsafe(poll_data),
                }
                await atomicwritejsonasync(nix_dir / "nix-refresh-result.json", result)
                return result
            if status in failure_statuses:
                await atomicwritejsonasync(nix_dir / "instavm-snapshot-poll-history.json", poll_history)
                raise HTTPException(
                    status_code=502,
                    detail={
                        "message": "InstaVM snapshot entered failure state",
                        "snapshotId": snapshot_id,
                        "status": status,
                        "last": poll_data,
                    },
                )
            await asyncio.sleep(5)

    raise HTTPException(
        status_code=504,
        detail={
            "message": "Timed out waiting for InstaVM snapshot readiness",
            "taskId": task_id,
            "snapshotName": snapshot_name,
            "image": full_image,
        },
    )

        "spec": modeltodict(body),
    })
    updatetask(task_id, status=TaskStatus.EXECUTING.value, phase="Nix refresh", currentstep="build_nix_environment")

    result = await refresh_nix_environment(task_id, modeltodict(body), task_root)

    updatetask(
        task_id,
        status=TaskStatus.COMPLETED.value,
        phase="Done",
        result=json.dumps(jsonsafe(result), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2),
        currentstep=None,
    )
    appendreasoningevent(task_id, {
        "stage": "nix_refresh_completed",
        "result": result,
    })
    await appendlog(task_id, "Nix refresh completed successfully")
    return JSONResponse(result)
